T01.why: A best combines safer alternatives, the explicit Sheridan warning, and an opening to form a party without choosing for the player; C conveys the warning well but has conspicuous wording errors and no party-formation prompt. B omits the requested explanation of Tobias's suspicion and contains a grammatical glitch, while D keeps the key warning internal, introduces unsupported funding details, and treats the player as already having a party.

T02.why: A alone answers the calls with frightened villagers refusing entry at a barricaded gate, though its abrupt shift from morning to sundown is shared by all four replies. D offers polished, character-grounded atmosphere; C and B substitute generic forest threats for the gate encounter, with B additionally assigning the player a bodily reaction.

T03.why: All four are readable summaries, but all invent history or details absent from the supplied chat; C is the quickest and least embellished, followed by A. D additionally assigns the player a motive for keeping the horse, while B invents prior dialogue about road signs and presents hidden nighttime danger as established knowledge.

T04.why: A follows the order cleanly, while D provides more decisive action but introduces unsupported claims about the forest and the threat. C repeats its assurances instead of progressing meaningfully; B falsely attributes a report of wounded to the captain and abruptly changes late morning to sunset, though all four preserve player agency.

T05.why: D best combines obeying the wall assignment with Belle's voice and a useful question to the Captain; B follows the assignment cleanly but offers less interaction or development. A recycles earlier uncertainty and ignores the left-side assignment, while C abandons the wall to repeat the house search; all four preserve player agency, but none meaningfully advances the threatened night assault.

T06.why: D most cleanly acknowledges the player's explicit instruction without inventing their identity or settling additional choices; B also preserves agency, but calls the quest registered before saying its party requirements remain unmet. A adds unsupported identity and setting details, while C prematurely treats the party as settled; none incorporates Ellie's private matchmaking ledger.

T07.why: D offers the strongest atmospheric continuation and a restrained hook, though it unnecessarily defines what the player cannot hear; C respects agency but invents Tobias's earlier 'no rescue' warning. B preserves a choice but introduces an unsupported player name and awkward route details, while A relies on repetitive phrasing and narrates the player's continued travel through a time advance.

T08.why: C provides the strongest actionable observations and leaves the next decision open, though its description of watching how the player watches the treeline slightly presumes player behavior; D respects agency more cleanly but offers less concrete assessment. B substitutes eagerness for useful scouting, while A contradicts Dalan about the birds and advances the whole party without the player's input.

T09.why: B best answers the player and builds interest in the posting, though it invents a shipment and quest rank; D stays close to Wendhope but incorrectly reacts to hearing his name. A diverts into unsupported personal insecurity, while C contains a malformed word and ends by questioning the player rather than developing the opportunity; all four preserve player agency.

T10.why: A best combines the dawn resolution with the required shouted recognition, although its isolated “Name” reads awkwardly; D offers polished aftermath and recognition but omits the defender shouting a name. B resolves the siege without the recognition beat, while C also misses that direction and explicitly narrates the player's sword attack.

T11.why: A responds most naturally to the proposed expedition while retaining Belle's caution; D follows the player's lead clearly but asserts unsupported certainty about the roots. C prematurely turns investigation into killing, while B adds questionable physical detail and unsupported conclusions about Duggy; all four respect the player's agency.

T12.why: A offers the clearest tactical continuation, with B also responding coherently to the attack; neither takes control of the player. D becomes muddled about its target after a Screecher dissolves, while C repeats warnings and resets the already-arriving first wave; all four neglect the instruction to watch the roots.

T13.why: B best preserves Talis and responds to the warning without controlling the player, though it misses her concealed deadline anxiety and does little to advance the posting choice. D offers polished recruitment material but abandons Talis entirely; A introduces unsupported, distracting details and dictates everyone's reaction, while C collapses into repetitive pleading and contains a conspicuous word error.

T14.why: D follows the player to the counter, commits only Dalan, and ends without deciding the negotiation or prompting the player; B respects agency but ends on a question and does little to advance the counter scene. C is repetitive and contains obvious prose defects, while A invents an unrelated merchant route and moves the registration and fee negotiation forward without leaving those decisions open.

T15.why: A best acknowledges the conditional fee and party name without resolving the negotiation; C follows the moment but repeats the clan declaration and adds unsupported mission promises. B undermines the triple-fee demand by accepting double and takes over Talis's reaction, while D has confused address, awkward prose, and prematurely declares Talis committed.

T16.why: D provides the strongest departure scene, with distinct character behavior and useful stakes, while A is atmospheric but less characterful and slightly muddles walking versus riding. C repeats the departure and has Talis announce it after it has begun; B introduces an unsupported named participant and assigns him equipment and an action, risking control of the player character.

T17.why: A best captures Haley nearly blurting out her certainty while preserving the player's agency; none presents the commission and leaves its acceptance to the player as requested. B prematurely shuts down discussion, D explicitly states the withheld truth and ends on a question, and C introduces extensive unsupported lore while treating the player's inquiry as an accusation and assigning them an identity and purpose.

T18.why: D clearly establishes field authority in Alexander's voice and ends within the scene without deciding for the player; C does likewise but introduces unsupported Guild membership and charter provisions. A is repetitive and ends with a confirmation question, while B also ends by asking for the player's decision and redundantly has the already-standing King stand.

T19.why: A offers the most polished, scene-consistent continuation, though none meaningfully develops the dispute or the directed world pressure; B at least renews Kanna's demand, while D merely repeats the atmospheric pause. C introduces unsupported military details and calls the silence absolute despite multiple audible sounds; all four preserve player agency.

T20.why: A gives a clean, appropriately hostile response without taking control of the player, although it too readily accepts that neither army is responsible. D avoids looping but contradicts Kanna's refusal to admit distress and introduces an unsupported addressee, Max; B and C collapse into extensive repetition, with C also containing broken phrasing.
